I found Q3.4 about Absalon data challenging because while I understand its potential benefits, I'm uncomfortable with the idea of being monitored so closely online.

The most important question for me was Q5.2: it's crucial that the model does a good job identifying students who need support, especially those who might be overlooked otherwise.

I noticed we unanimously rejected using race/ethnicity data (Q3.5), but opinions varied more on disability-related information and financial aid status. I chose "moderate" for disability because it might help identify students with specific needs; I'm not sure why others were okay with no threshold or only small improvement.

I wonder if an opt-out mechanism could address some concerns, allowing students to choose their comfort level with data usage.

Thank you for sharing your thoughts.

I also found Q3.4 difficult because tracking online activity feels intrusive. I agree that Q5.2 is crucial; ensuring the model effectively identifies students who need support is essential.

Our unanimous rejection of race/ethnicity data (Q3.5) makes sense, but opinions varied on disability-related information. I chose "moderate" for disability because it could help identify students with specific needs who might require additional support. Financial aid status also seemed important to many, and I agreed, as financial struggles can impact academic performance.

An opt-out mechanism is a good idea—it could allow students to control their data usage while still benefiting from the support system.

I found Q3.4 challenging because monitoring online activity feels invasive, especially since I'm still adapting to Danish university systems and don't want my learning process to be scrutinized so closely.

The most important questions for me were around data privacy (Q3) and explainability (Q4). Understanding why a student is flagged as at-risk is crucial for providing appropriate support and building trust, especially when dealing with sensitive issues.

I noticed we unanimously rejected using race/ethnicity data (Q3.5), which makes sense given its sensitivity. However, opinions varied on disability-related information. I chose "never" because I believe it's too invasive and could lead to stigmatization or discrimination. An opt-out mechanism might help address some privacy concerns, but I think we should also consider the ethical implications of using any sensitive data in predictive models.

As a student advisor, being able to explain why a student was flagged is crucial for providing effective support. Trust is essential in these conversations, and we need to ensure that the model's decisions can be clearly communicated.

I noticed that while we unanimously rejected using race/ethnicity data, opinions varied on disability-related information. I chose "moderate" because I believe it could help identify students with specific needs who might require additional support. However, I also recognize the sensitivity of this data and the importance of handling it carefully. An opt-out mechanism could be a good solution to address some concerns while still allowing the model to provide valuable insights.

Overall, I think we need to strike a balance between using data to support students and respecting their privacy and autonomy.
